title: 2026 Policy Agenda
plain_title: The building industry's 2026 policy priorities for New York
what_they_audited: An annual policy agenda from the New York Building Congress, a construction industry membership association, setting out the proposals it will push for in 2026. Items are labeled as federal, state or city, and cover infrastructure funding, housing, transportation, energy, resilience, procurement, workforce and technology.
background: The group describes itself as a membership association that brings together architects, engineers, contractors, subcontractors, labor, owners and consultants, and it says the federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law expires in 2026.

findings.plain: The group names three top priorities for the year: a new federal surface transportation funding bill, changes to the 485-x housing tax break, and sustained capital budgets for state and city agencies including the Metropolitan Transportation Authority and the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey.

recommendations: Release federal infrastructure money faster and give New York a share reflecting its population, transit systems and contribution to federal taxes and gross domestic product.
Add worker training provisions to the next federal infrastructure bill, including new grants for industry partnerships and H-1B visa cap exemptions for government-funded infrastructure work.
Track and disclose federal infrastructure spending more fully.
Streamline and speed up environmental reviews and permitting for infrastructure projects at every level of government, and adopt changes that reduce construction costs.
Stabilize the federal Highway Trust Fund with predictable revenue so states can plan multi-year projects.
Write lasting changes to the National Environmental Policy Act into law and widen the set of projects that qualify for categorical exclusions, supporting the SPEED Act and the RESTART Act.
Expand the categories of actions exempt from review under the State Environmental Quality Review Act and adopt the state bill creating exemptions for qualifying infill and transit-oriented housing.

Create a National Infrastructure Reserve Board, an independent body modeled on the Federal Reserve with a standing appropriation, to fund state-of-good-repair and replacement needs outside the annual budget cycle.
Reevaluate, expand and fine-tune the 485-x zones for projects of 150 units or more, vary the income and wage requirements by neighborhood, and add a new bracket for the largest projects.
Treat projects using 485-x as Type 2 actions under the State Environmental Quality Review Act.
Fast-track environmental assessments for new housing and housing-related infrastructure.
Allow affordable housing to be built as of right in districts where less than 10 percent of housing rents below market.
Extend zoning exemptions in Special Transit Land Use Districts to a full half mile around each transit zone, as in the original City of Yes proposal.
Have state lawmakers prioritize senior housing in the suburbs.
Create the NYC Affordability Fund proposed by the city comptroller, deploying about $2.5 billion in pension capital toward up to 75,000 affordable homes.
Keep and expand the incentives behind office-to-residential conversions, including the City of Yes changes and the 467-m program.

Create an Interborough Express transit-oriented development special district covering land within a half mile of each planned station, and set up a Rail-to-Roof air rights market that lets nearby owners sell unused floor area into that district.
Adopt a statewide transit-oriented development framework modeled on the Massachusetts MBTA Communities law, with base densities above 15 units per acre.

For the Manhattan plan, raise residential floor area in the Special Hudson Yards District from 4 to at least 18, raise floor area around 125th Street ahead of Second Avenue Subway phase 2, reexamine historic districts for where more housing could go, sharply raise residential floor area caps to enable office conversions in districts such as the Financial District and Midtown, and deck over roadways such as the FDR Drive and tunnel approaches for housing.

Expand the budget of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, specifically Community Development Block Grants, the HOME Investment Partnerships Program and the Public Housing Capital Fund, and support the Pro-Housing Act, the INCREASE Housing Affordability Act and the Build More Housing Near Transit Act.

Accelerate the Brooklyn Marine Terminal project, including swift state approval of the General Project Plan and a federal decision to review it through an environmental assessment rather than a full environmental impact statement.
Speed up MTA change orders and invoice payments and create a formal feedback loop with the building industry to identify bottlenecks.
Rebalance risk in MTA contracts, including insurance, indemnification and bonding terms, so more qualified firms bid.
Use qualifications-based selection for MTA procurements, giving technical merit more weight with transparent scoring.
Commit to full Americans with Disabilities Act compliance across the MTA network, prioritizing high-ridership and transfer stations and publishing timelines and progress.
Expand transit-oriented development tools such as Zoning for Accessibility so private development helps pay for station accessibility while adding housing.

Fund the Gateway Program, advance the Penn Station overhaul, start Second Avenue Subway phase 2 and plan phase 3 and a 125th Street crosstown extension, advance Interborough Express design and environmental work, and pursue a full redesign of the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway with federal funding commitments.
Reuse the abandoned LIRR Rockaway Beach Branch between Rego Park and Ozone Park for both a new subway connection and a park.
Increase state funding for renewable energy projects, including onshore and offshore wind and a renewable energy hub on Rikers Island after the jails close.

Create a state-financed renewable energy fund in the budget rather than funding upgrades through utility ratepayers, pointing to bills that would tax large crypto miners and create a separate utility class for large data centers.

Shorten permitting and grid interconnection timelines at NYISO and the Office of Renewable Energy Siting and Electric Transmission, add staff, and treat clean energy projects as Type 2 actions under the State Environmental Quality Review Act.
Prioritize transmission upgrades, including directing the New York Power Authority to invest in them.
Increase funding and incentives for battery storage.
Encourage renewable natural gas where electrification is difficult and allow blending.
Run streamlined NYSERDA procurements with quarterly solicitations for large-scale renewables.
Expand large-scale geothermal in New York City through more funding, technical support and inclusion in long-term capital and energy planning.

Fully implement the streamlined federal licensing created by the ADVANCE Act to deploy advanced nuclear facilities such as small modular reactors, and support the state's 5 gigawatt nuclear goal and its advanced nuclear master plan.
Advance planning and design for the Army Corps of Engineers' New York and New Jersey Harbor and Tributaries study of storm surge barriers.
Increase the Clean Water State Revolving Fund to finance water infrastructure upgrades.
Continue the Lower Manhattan Coastal Resiliency project.
Strengthen sewage and drainage systems, targeting neighborhood-scale green infrastructure and Bluebelt-style drainage upgrades in areas that flood repeatedly.

Keep practical exemptions, flexibility and clearer good-faith guidance in Local Law 97, particularly for public health and safety facilities and nonprofits, and earmark noncompliance penalties for grid improvements or energy-efficiency retrofits.
Streamline land use reviews for hospitals and related health care facilities, along the lines of the City of Yes zoning changes.
Give health care facilities flexible Local Law 97 compliance schedules.
Create a protocol that automatically adjusts emissions calculations for health care facilities when utilities require or recommend changes in energy use during grid instability.
Improve hiring at New York City agencies by speeding up Office of Management and Budget review and approval of positions and making salaries more competitive with the private sector.
Add engineering and technical staff at the New York City comptroller's office to speed dispute determinations and improve communication about claim status.
Streamline payment requisitions and change order processing across all procurement agencies.

Create a set of pre-approved best practices for contract processes that any procurement department can adopt, with the Office of Management and Budget giving agencies flexibility to choose the approach that fits a project.
Add requisition numbers to city payments on Checkbook NYC.
Shorten bid cycles and clarify procurement so firms can recruit and retain staff.
Set more project funding as multi-year commitments with clear capital plans.
Reduce insurance and indemnification requirements so pricing reflects actual project risk.
Change the Dormitory Authority of the State of New York's procurement and risk requirements and allow public-private partnership models for university facilities.

Have government agencies buy and store critical materials up front for large projects, include larger contingency line items for material price escalation, and offer tax credits when material costs rise enough to stall a project.

Convert the New York City Department of Design and Construction into a public authority, modeled on the School Construction Authority, with multi-year bonding capacity and flexibility in project delivery methods.
Have the state authorize one-step progressive design-build for all project types and city agencies, and remove cost from the evaluation criteria for those procurements.
Expand CM-Build beyond the project types the Department of Design and Construction may now use it for, and make it available to all city agencies.
Continue the New York City Capital Process Reform Task Force under the new administration.
Have the state legislature extend authorization for joint bidding in city procurements.
Guarantee timely contract payments, especially to minority and women-owned business enterprises.
Make minority and women-owned business enterprise certification reciprocal between the state and New York City.
Create a single centralized procurement portal for minority and women-owned business enterprises across government entities.

Create a federal H-1B visa cap exemption and fast-track approval program for government-funded infrastructure, targeted at United States-educated workers in fields such as engineering, architecture, construction management and planning.
Fund childcare centers that open at 6 a.m. so early work hours do not keep people out of the workforce.
Lower fees for federal certification and required training courses, particularly those from the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
Expand Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act programs for youth, adults and dislocated workers.
Increase funding for public and nonprofit apprenticeship, STEAM education and job training programs in all five boroughs, and increase support for statewide training programs.
Have state lawmakers create an artificial intelligence in construction and engineering task force, with the group's innovation council represented.
Require a standard 'Human Reviewed' certification on drawings, blueprints and project plans, and set industry-wide best practices for human oversight.

Fully build out the city's 3D underground mapping initiative as a central, city-run repository of subsurface data in BIM-compatible formats, generally meeting or exceeding Quality Level B under the ASCE 38-22 standard.
